clue.text: One causes panic having limb stuck in a register

indicators.note: something stuck in something else is lodged inside it, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: taken as written
a list is a register of names
an arm is a limb

explanation.surface: Someone panics because their arm is jammed in a cash register.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A register' together gives A LIST, and the limb goes between its second and third letters to make ALARMIST.
explanation.definitionFit: An alarmist is a person who spreads needless fear and stirs up worry in others.

clue.text: Working to bring back musical about college

indicators.note: bringing something back returns it the way it came, so the letters run the other direction
to be about something is to surround it, so one piece wraps another

parts.note: Evita is the Lloyd Webber musical
C is a standard abbreviation for college

explanation.surface: A producer wants to revive a show about university life.
explanation.walkthrough: C sits inside EVITA to give EVITCA, which read backwards is ACTIVE.
explanation.definitionFit: A machine or person that is working is busy, functioning and in operation, the sense of active.

clue.text: River that delivers so much!

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the great South American river
second meaning: the online retailer whose parcels arrive everywhere

explanation.walkthrough: A river 'delivers' a huge volume of water to the sea, which hides the second sense: the giant internet shop famous for its deliveries.
explanation.definitionFit: The same name belongs to the vast South American waterway and to the online shopping company that ships goods worldwide.

clue.text: Russian fighter helping people moving

parts.note: a MiG is a Russian fighter jet
a helping of food is a ration, a portion

explanation.surface: A Russian soldier assists people who are relocating.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Russian fighter' reads like a soldier, but it is the aircraft; 'helping' is a noun, a portion, not a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Migration is the movement of populations from one region or country to settle in another.

clue.text: Massage so dear, mostly — that's just typical

indicators.note: to massage figures is to manipulate them, so the letters that follow are worked into a new order

parts.note: every letter of these three words is used, including the word for most of

explanation.surface: Someone grumbles that an expensive massage is, as usual, mostly overpriced.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Massage' looks like the subject, and 'mostly' looks like an instruction to drop a letter, but it belongs to the fodder in full.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an exasperated idiom for a familiar, predictable situation that keeps recurring.

clue.text: Good little fellows make GIs?

parts.note: G is the abbreviation for good
runts are undersized people or animals

explanation.surface: A question whether well-behaved small men turn into American soldiers.
explanation.walkthrough: GIs are American soldiers; the setter needs the US slang term for an ordinary infantryman.
explanation.definitionFit: Grunt is American military slang for a low-ranking foot soldier, just as GI is.

clue.text: River starts to rise here in northern Europe

indicators.note: the starts of words are their opening letters, so only those are kept

parts.note: the opening letter of each of the five words

explanation.surface: A river begins at its source somewhere in northern Europe.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as geography about a river's source, which is exactly what disguises the first-letter device.
explanation.definitionFit: The Rhine is a major European waterway flowing from the Alps to the North Sea.

clue.text: It's said to deny being feverish when unwell

definitions.meaning: first meaning, read literally: claiming one's temperature is not high
second meaning: the idiom for feeling poorly

explanation.walkthrough: Taken word by word, the phrase denies a high temperature, yet as an idiom it means feeling ill, so the two senses pull against each other.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying you feel less than great is an informal idiom for being a bit poorly or under the weather.

clue.text: Pleasing arrangement that doesn't change on reflection?

definitions.text: Pleasing arrangement that doesn't change on reflection?

parts.note: surface reading: an opinion or plan that stays firm after careful thought

parts.words: Pleasing arrangement that doesn't change on reflection?
parts.note: setter's reading: a balanced shape that looks identical when mirrored

explanation.walkthrough: 'Reflection' suggests thinking things over; the setter means a mirror image, which a balanced design survives unchanged.
explanation.definitionFit: Mirror balance is the property of a shape that matches itself across an axis, often found visually pleasing.

clue.text: It requires fellow players giving support to hold back dangerous stuff

indicators.note: to hold something is to grip it inside, so one piece surrounds another

parts.note: a tee is the peg supporting a golf ball

indicators.note: going back means moving in the opposite direction, so the letters run right to left

parts.note: magma is molten rock, dangerous indeed

explanation.surface: A team effort is needed to contain a hazardous substance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hold back' looks like a single phrase for restraining, but 'back' turns the molten rock round and 'to hold' puts it inside the golf peg.
explanation.definitionFit: Football or hockey, for example, need several players cooperating on one side, unlike solo sports.

clue.text: Casualty of never-ending evil period

indicators.note: something with no ending has lost its last part, so each word is cut short at the tail

parts.note: vice, an evil, without its final letter
time, a period, without its final letter

explanation.surface: Someone suffers harm during an endless era of wickedness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Never-ending' applies to both following words: vice and time each lose their last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A casualty is someone injured or killed, a person who suffers harm, just as a victim does.

clue.text: He detests Tim working and holds things back

indicators.note: letters that are working are being put to use and moved about, so they take a new order

parts.note: all twelve letters of these three words

explanation.surface: A man who loathes his colleague Tim at work keeps obstructing things.
explanation.walkthrough: The sentence reads as office feud; the three opening words are pure fodder and 'working' is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means halting or checking a flow or trend, figuratively restraining something advancing.

clue.text: Instrument giving chord, flat essentially

indicators.note: the essence of a word is its core, so only the central letters are kept

parts.note: the central pair of a six-letter word
the central letter of a five-letter word
the central pair of a four-letter word

explanation.surface: A musical instrument plays a chord that comes out flat.
explanation.walkthrough: The musical words 'chord' and 'flat' suggest music theory, but 'essentially' takes the middles of 'giving', 'chord' and 'flat' alike.
explanation.definitionFit: The viola is a stringed member of the violin family, slightly larger and lower in pitch.

clue.text: Place bet? Not if it's this accurate

definitions.text: Place bet? Not if it's this
definitions.meaning: first meaning: a racing wager to win only, the opposite of backing a horse to be placed
second meaning: the idiom for exactly right

explanation.walkthrough: In horse racing a place bet pays if the horse finishes in the top few; a bet that only pays on outright victory is described by this phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes something precise or exact, hitting the target with no margin of error.

clue.text: Roam semi-nude when drunk, giving slight offence

indicators.note: drunk people stagger about in disorder, so the letters lose their original order

parts.note: all the letters of these two words

explanation.surface: Wandering about half-naked while intoxicated is a minor breach of the law.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is an apt picture of a minor crime, which is what the answer names.
explanation.definitionFit: A misdemeanour is a minor wrongdoing or lesser crime, less serious than a felony.

clue.text: A bishop disgraced, having refused to take part

parts.note: taken as written
B is the chess abbreviation for bishop
a stained reputation is a disgraced one

explanation.surface: A disgraced bishop stays out of the vote.
explanation.walkthrough: B for bishop is the chess notation; 'disgraced' becomes a past participle meaning tarnished.
explanation.definitionFit: To abstain is to decline to vote or participate, so this past tense matches refusal to join in.

clue.text: Keeps down bears

definitions.meaning: first meaning: holds food in without vomiting
second meaning: tolerates or puts up with

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests suppressing large animals; both words are verbs, one about digestion and one about tolerance.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb covers both retaining food without being sick and enduring something unpleasant.

clue.text: Dogs like frolicking where there's snow outside

indicators.note: frolicking is playing about wildly, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: all the letters of these two words

explanation.surface: Dogs love playing about in the snow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Like' looks like a verb of enjoyment, but it is just letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A chalet at a mountain resort sits amid wintry slopes, so snow lies all around it.

clue.text: Beginning to enjoy work in carpeting

parts.note: starting to like something is taking to it
a task is a piece of work

explanation.surface: Someone starts to enjoy a job laying carpets.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain, carpeting someone means giving them a dressing-down, originally being summoned onto the boss's carpet.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases mean severely reprimanding someone for a fault, a stern telling-off.

clue.text: Ordinary company working to acquire millions

indicators.note: acquiring something means taking it in, so one piece ends up inside the others

parts.note: CO is the abbreviation for company
M stands for million, doubled for the plural
a machine that is on is working

explanation.surface: An everyday firm in business sets out to make millions.
explanation.walkthrough: Plurals are often shown by doubling an abbreviation, as with pp for pages, so millions is MM.
explanation.definitionFit: Common and ordinary are synonyms describing something usual, everyday and unremarkable.

clue.text: One coming out over master getting promoted? That's rubbish

parts.note: a deb, short for debutante, is a young woman coming out into society

indicators.note: being promoted means going up, and in a down entry going up turns the letters upside down

parts.note: sir is a form of address for a master

explanation.surface: Someone emerging after their boss is promoted calls it all nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: A debutante 'comes out' at her first society ball; 'over' places her above the upturned SIR in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Debris is scattered waste or remains, so it is a synonym for rubbish or litter.

clue.text: Criminal mob rule North East city

indicators.note: something criminal is crooked, so these letters are bent into a new order

parts.note: the letters of both words
NE is the compass abbreviation for north-east

explanation.surface: Gangsters take control of a city in north-east England.
explanation.walkthrough: 'North East city' suggests Newcastle or Sunderland; the city is in Australia and NE just finishes it.
explanation.definitionFit: Melbourne is a large Australian metropolis, the state capital of Victoria.

clue.text: It's shocking to get incorrect order regularly

parts.note: a calculation that is out is wrong

indicators.note: at regular intervals means every other one, so alternate letters are kept

parts.note: the second and fourth letters

explanation.surface: Getting an order wrong all the time is appalling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Incorrect order' looks like an anagram instruction, but 'incorrect' supplies a word meaning wrong and 'order' is thinned to its even letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Outré describes something bizarre or unconventional, far enough beyond accepted norms to startle people.

clue.text: Roused in astonishment having received permission…

indicators.note: receiving something means taking it in, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: awe is wonder or astonishment
an OK is a go-ahead

explanation.surface: Someone is startled awake on being given approval.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links the story into the next clue but plays no part in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Roused and awoke both describe coming out of sleep, past tense of waking someone or oneself.

clue.text: …bad guys imprison alien recruits

indicators.note: to imprison is to lock someone inside, so one piece is enclosed by another

parts.note: cads are dishonourable men
ET is the film alien

explanation.surface: Villains lock up an extraterrestrial who has signed up.
explanation.walkthrough: A cad is an old-fashioned British word for a man who behaves badly, especially towards women.
explanation.definitionFit: Cadets are trainees in the military or police, new entrants learning the service.

clue.text: Skinflint has no money? That's the wrong description

indicators.note: to have something is to hold it, so one piece holds the others

parts.note: a miser is a stingy hoarder
taken as written
M is an abbreviation for money

explanation.surface: Calling a tightwad penniless would be inaccurate, since misers are usually rich.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is nicely self-referential: a miser claiming poverty is exactly a false label.
explanation.definitionFit: A misnomer is an inaccurate or misleading name applied to something.

clue.text: Slow eastward expansion emptied a country

indicators.note: an emptied container has lost its contents, so only the outside letters remain

parts.note: first and last letters
first and last letters
first and last letters

explanation.surface: A nation slowly spreads its territory towards the east.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Emptied' applies to all three preceding words, each reduced to its two outer letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Sweden is a Scandinavian nation in northern Europe, whose capital is Stockholm.

clue.text: Sticklers will want name removed from such jewellery

indicators.note: taking something out of a word implies it sat inside, so solvers put it back in to build the solution

parts.note: pedants insist on fussy correctness
N is the abbreviation for name

explanation.surface: Fussy people would insist on taking the engraved name off their necklaces.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue works backwards: lose the N from the jewellery and you are left with the sticklers, so N goes inside them to reach the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A pendant is a piece of jewellery hanging from a chain around the neck.
